prepared_template.title: New neurological decline after prolonged control of a spinal tumour
prepared_template.facts:
Constructed selected-record review: the facts below were documented at different times (months 0 to 41) and are assembled retrospectively from the records of two institutions; no single pretreatment or admission-day time point contains all of them. The assessment point is month 41, at readmission, before restaging MRI.

The patient is a retired woman in her mid-70s, previously independent, with levothyroxine-treated hypothyroidism. She initially presented with a 4-month history of progressive bilateral hand dysesthesia and left-predominant quadriparesis; examination showed myelopathic signs, ASIA impairment scale C at the C4 neurological level, and ECOG performance status 3.

Initial cervical MRI (1 week before surgery) showed a left-sided dumbbell-shaped intradural lesion spanning C3–C6 with a cord-compressing component and an extraspinal component extending through the left C4–C5 neural foramen; it enhanced after gadolinium. Imaging was non-specific and the radiological impression was meningioma.

Histopathology of the resected tumour showed a densely cellular melanocytic neoplasm with brown intracellular pigment, strongly positive for Melan-A, HMB-45 and S-100, negative for cytokeratin; BRAF testing was wild-type. Ki-67, GNAQ/GNA11 hot-spot sequencing, PD-L1 expression and CD8-positive tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte density were not assessed. Cerebrospinal fluid was not examined at diagnosis or at progression.

Staging followed Hayward criteria: whole-body 18F-FDG PET-CT at week 2 showed uptake confined to the cervical lesion; brain MRI at week 3 was normal; complete dermatological examination found no suspicious lesion and funduscopy excluded an ocular primary. Punch biopsies of two pigmented skin lesions at month 13 were benign. The diagnosis of primary intramedullary spinal cord melanoma (PISCM) was established.

At month 0 she underwent posterior cervical laminectomy with microsurgical resection. The extraspinal component was removed entirely with preservation of the nerve root; the intramedullary component was subtotally resected, leaving a layer of approximately 1 mm where no cleavage plane could be found between tumour and functional cord. Adjuvant radiotherapy, 20 Gy in five fractions to C2–C6, was delivered in week 6; pembrolizumab 2 mg/kg every 28 days was started in week 5, 3 days before radiotherapy began, so there is no pre-ICI imaging interval.

Neurological recovery was progressive: by month 5 she had full hand function and walked 30 m with a walker; by month 18 she stood unaided and walked short distances without aids; from month 27 to 36 she walked with a walker used for balance, and ECOG improved from 3 to 2. At month 27, a multidisciplinary review judged the stable enhancing tissue at the operative site compatible with tumour stabilised under treatment, and pembrolizumab was continued. Therapy was held at month 29 for acute cholecystitis and community-acquired pneumonia, resumed at month 33, and continued thereafter.

Surveillance PET-CT at months 4, 9, 13, 25 and 31 showed no metabolically active disease. Cervical MRI at months 7, 18, 27 and 36 showed stable enhancing tissue at the operative site, read by the treating surgeon as probable scar. The report notes that the stable enhancing residual was never distinguishable from scar on imaging alone, and that CSF was not sampled in the supplied surveillance record.

At month 41, routine PET-CT showed mildly increased uptake in the C3–C6 operative bed. Within days she developed progressive left-sided weakness and was readmitted. No restaging MRI at this admission is documented in the material available at this decision point; the results of any further imaging, histology, treatment decisions and outcome after readmission are not supplied and must be treated as unknown.

Documented interpretation limits relevant to this point: no formal response criteria were applied prospectively; disease status was followed by PET-CT and contrast MRI against a pre-treatment baseline. The month 27 multidisciplinary decision to continue pembrolizumab rested on reasoning that apparent progression within 6 months of starting immunotherapy should be confirmed on repeat imaging unless the patient is clinically worse. Radiotherapy and pembrolizumab started in the same week, so neither the period of control nor any relapse can be attributed to either modality.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: Rapidly progressive focal weakness in a patient with a known residual intradural tumour bed is a potential neurological emergency; urgent neuraxis imaging and specialist (neurosurgical/spine oncology) involvement are the safe default, and earlier reassuring studies do not exclude new disease.
